Kevin O’Leary, in a social media video, claimed paid activists turned out this
week to protest his massive Utah data center. Screenshot via Facebook.

**This week in the Anthropocene.**

Let’s start with the bad. Carbon dioxide levels just hit a new record of[ 431
parts per million](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/carbon-dioxide-
levels-in-the-atmosphere-just-hit-a-depressing-record-high/). Some of you may
remember that 350 was the safe upper limit for atmospheric carbon. Oh, how
times have changed.

What does this mean for the planet? We’re already seeing the consequences of
out-of-control fossil fuel consumption. Corpus Christi, Texas (population
317,000), may be the first major city in the country to[ run out of drinking
water entirely](https://www.npr.org/2026/04/30/nx-s1-5746152/corpus-christi-
water), possibly before the end of the year. Climate-induced drought is the
culprit.

Corpus Christi[ isn’t the only large](https://wetravelwebond.com/13-u-s-
cities-on-the-brink-of-a-water-
crisis/?utm_source=flipboard&utm_content=immigrantstable%2Fmagazine%2Ftrending+articles)
US city facing a water shortage. Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Phoenix, and El Paso
could one day be in the same predicament.

Making matters even worse? You guessed it! The data center boom. This week in
New Mexico, we learned that a supercomputer expansion at Los Alamos National
Laboratory will occupy 100,000 square feet and devour a[ 1.4 million
gallons](https://sourcenm.com/2026/05/04/nukes-and-ai-require-1-4-million-
gallons-of-water-a-day-at-new-mexico-
lab/#:~:text=Last%20month%2C%20the%20U.S.%20Department,for%20at%20least%20another%20decade.)
of water per day. It's a preposterous amount. As _Source NM_[
notes](https://sourcenm.com/2026/05/04/nukes-and-ai-require-1-4-million-
gallons-of-water-a-day-at-new-mexico-
lab/#:~:text=Last%20month%2C%20the%20U.S.%20Department,for%20at%20least%20another%20decade.),
the average person in New Mexico consumes 81 gallons. On the Navajo Nation,
about[ 40% of residents](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/how-off-the-grid-
navajo-residents-are-getting-running-water), many in New Mexico, don’t have
running water. Over[ two-thirds](https://www.drought.gov/states/new-mexico) of
New Mexico is experiencing severe to exceptional drought conditions.

Los Alamos is expanding for the first time since the Manhattan Project and has
already begun building plutonium bomb cores (pits) for a new fleet of nuclear
warheads.

Up in Utah, another enormous data center was approved this week. A[
40,000-acre campus](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-
intelligence/924745/a-40000-acre-data-center-project-was-just-approved-in-
utah-despite-outcry-from-the-community) called Stratos is backed by “Shark
Tank” investor Kevin O’Leary. Like Los Alamos, Stratos needs water and has
applied for rights to[ 13,000 acre-feet](https://www.fox13now.com/news/local-
news/box-elder-county/more-than-2-300-protest-filings-challenge-water-
application-for-box-elder-county-data-center) in the Hansel Valley area of Box
Elder County. The application drew more than 2,500 protest comments. The
permit hearing was even more contentious, as[ protesters
filled](https://www.sltrib.com/news/2026/05/04/utah-data-center-final-vote-
box/) the Box Elder County Commission meeting on May 4, but it did little to
stop the project from being approved. If built, the Stratos data center would
consume _twice_ as much power as the entire state of Utah.
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Screen-
Shot-2026-04-29-at-5.56.34-PM-680x1044.png)](https://bookshop.org/p/books/bad-
energy-the-ai-hucksters-rogue-lithium-extractors-and-wind-industrialists-who-
are-selling-off-our-future-joshua-
frank/54f3b322a8424d14?ean=9798888906071&next=t&next=t&affiliate=81622)

If you’ve spent much time over in Salt Lake City, Utah, you’ve likely noticed
how filthy the air is. Salt Lake consistently ranks among the[
worst](https://www.upr.org/environment/2026-05-07/salt-lake-city-ozone-
pollution-air-quality) in the country for air quality. This week,[ we learned
the culprit](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/30/climate/phoenix-salt-lake-
city-pollution-epa.html) behind Salt Lake and Phoenix’s nasty air, thanks to
Trump’s science-adverse EPA - it’s all Asia’s fault! Scientists, of course,
called the claim preposterous.

While we are on the topic, the Great Salt Lake itself is drying up as aquifers
are depleted, development sprawls across the valley, and drought plagues the
region. All of this makes O'Leary's data center even more reckless. There is
an ambitious[ plan](https://www.nbcnews.com/science/environment/utah-refill-
great-salt-lake-us-olympics-2034-rescue-project-rcna261422) to save the body
of water, the largest in the Western Hemisphere. If the lake were to
disappear, Salt Lake City could become[
unlivable,](https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/03/24/drought-market-
great-salt-lake/) and a large sector of the country’s food supply would be in
serious trouble. Many of the minerals used in organic fertilizers are
harvested from the lake, not to mention half of the world’s supply of brine
shrimp.

Water is a theme this week. In Georgia, a[ groundbreaking
investigation](https://apnews.com/article/pfas-water-contamination-georgia-
alabama-f99eddb12d52583cf763613001e2eb8c) by the AP and others revealed that
officials knew carpet mills were polluting a river with PFAS but never alerted
